cards.hook: VIX futures usually cost more the longer you wait.

cards.body: In calm regimes the VIX term structure sits in **contango**: each further-out future prices above spot. A long-vol position holding those futures loses a little every day as each one rolls down toward a lower spot, whether or not volatility ever rises. Reported figures put VIX futures in contango roughly 75 to 85% of trading days. That roll cost is why buy-and-hold VIX products decay toward zero, and why long vol is a timing trade, not a hold.
cards.depth: The mirror image is backwardation in a panic, when near-term fear prices above the curve and the roll pays you instead. So the same structure that bleeds in calm markets pays in a crash. Sizing long vol means budgeting the daily roll as an insurance premium you are paying, not treating a flat tape as a free hold.

cards.hook: The next AI-training fight is about dilution, not copying.
cards.body: In the 2025 training cases, courts leaned toward calling the copying itself transformative. What tripped plaintiffs up was the fourth fair-use factor, market harm. A federal judge in a 2025 Meta case suggested the strongest theory is **market dilution**: not that the model copied your book, but that its cheap synthetic substitutes flood and depress the market you sell into. The copying got waved through; the live question is whether a model trained on you can then compete you out of existence.
cards.depth: This flips litigation strategy. Plaintiffs need evidence of a real substitution market, foreclosed licensing, or measurable price erosion, not just proof their work sat in the training set. Defendants win by showing outputs do not compete in the same market. Discovery shifts from what did you ingest to what does your output displace.

cards.hook: After the fact, you'll swear you saw it coming.
cards.body: Once you know the outcome, memory quietly rewrites your earlier estimate to look smarter, an effect called **hindsight bias**. A 40% call becomes 'I basically knew it.' The damage is not vanity. It is that you can never learn calibration from a memory that edits itself, because every past forecast now feels well-judged. The only defense is a timestamped record of what you actually predicted, made before the result existed to contaminate it.
cards.depth: This is why a written prediction log beats honest reflection. It also explains why post-mortems blame people: once the failure is known, the warning signs look obvious and someone should have caught them. They were not obvious inside the decision. Judge the process against what was knowable then, not against what you know now.

cards.hook: Your ADHD med is inert until your blood cuts it apart.
cards.body: Lisdexamfetamine is dexamphetamine bolted to the amino acid lysine, and it does nothing until enzymes in your red blood cells cleave that lysine off. The conversion is **rate-limited by your blood, not a pill coating**, which is why onset is gradual and the tail is even. Two consequences follow: dose it early, because it ramps slowly and you want it working by morning, and do not bother splitting or crushing it, because the bottleneck is enzymatic, not the capsule.
cards.depth: The same enzymatic gate is why the dose-response is steadier from person to person and why the drug is harder to misuse. It also means a 'barely noticeable' read in the first days is expected, not failure. Judge titration over weeks, at a fixed daily time, never by the verdict of one morning.

cards.hook: Recall it: which shorts in your backtest could never be borrowed?
cards.body: The winners a long-short backtest loves are often the hardest-to-borrow names: small, distressed, heavily shorted, exactly the stocks a broker will not lend you or will lend only at punishing fees. Your backtest assumes free, unlimited borrow. **The edge lived in trades you could never actually place.** The fix is to filter your short universe to liquid, borrowable names, or subtract realistic borrow costs, then see how much alpha was a lending fantasy.
cards.depth: The same illusion appears on the long side as capacity: a signal that prints on micro-caps evaporates once your size moves the price. Both are execution ceilings the backtest silently ignores. A returns curve is only as real as the trades beneath it were fillable at the prices it assumed.

cards.hook: The option smile leans because crashes cluster and rallies don't.
cards.body: Equity index puts trade at higher implied vol than equidistant calls. Retail calls it fear pricing, and fear is part of it. The deeper reason is that index returns are genuinely negatively skewed. Big down days arrive with volatility spikes and correlations racing toward one, while rallies grind slowly. So downside strikes really do sit on more variance, and sellers price that asymmetry in. **The skew is a forecast of the return distribution's shape, not just a sentiment tax.** Treat a flattening skew as the market repricing crash odds, not as free premium.
cards.depth: Mechanically, the leverage effect and forced deleveraging make volatility itself rise when prices fall, so a put hedges two things at once, direction and the vol spike that rides along with it. That double duty is what a call the same distance away cannot offer, and it is why the smirk rarely vanishes in a healthy equity index.

cards.hook: SAG-AFTRA splits digital replicas in two, and consent must be specific.
cards.body: The 2023 TV and theatrical contract drew a line practitioners still blur. An employment-based digital replica is built from a performer's work during their engagement. An independently created one is made outside it, from other material. Both require the performer's clear consent and separate pay, and that consent has to carry a **reasonably specific description of the intended use**. A buried, all-purpose grant does not cut it. So the drafting question is no longer whether you can make a replica, but whether your consent language survives that specificity test.
cards.depth: This is why studio AI riders now read like scope-of-license clauses. They enumerate mediums, projects, and duration rather than granting replica rights at large. The parallel for any deal lawyer is right-of-publicity licensing, where a vague grant has always been construed against the drafter. Specificity is not caution here, it is the enforceability requirement.

cards.hook: The fix worked because you tried it at rock bottom.
cards.body: Any extreme reading is part signal and part luck. When you act at the worst moment, the next measurement drifts back toward your true average on its own, and your intervention takes the credit. This is **regression to the mean**, and it fakes cause and effect everywhere. Kahneman watched flight instructors conclude that scolding a bad landing helped and praising a great one backfired. Both were just regression. A terrible landing was likely to be followed by a better one regardless, and a superb one by a worse one. Distrust any before-and-after that started at an extreme.
cards.depth: The trading version is obvious once you see it. A system tweaked right after its worst drawdown usually rebounds, and the tweak looks brilliant. Run the counterfactual. Would the untouched system have recovered anyway? Often yes. The only clean test is a control, a comparison to what the same starting point does when you change nothing at all.

cards.hook: A perfect oil hedge went bankrupt on its own margin calls.
cards.body: In the early 1990s a Metallgesellschaft unit sold long-dated fixed-price contracts to deliver oil for years, then hedged by holding a stack of near-month futures it kept rolling forward. On paper the price risk was covered. Then oil fell. The futures threw off immediate margin calls in cash, while the offsetting gains on the delivery contracts would not arrive until far in the future. The hedge was directionally sound and still nearly sank the company, reportedly around a $1.3 billion loss. **A hedge that is right on price can still kill you on timing.**
cards.depth: The second wound was the term structure. The stack-and-roll earned money while the market stayed in backwardation, but the curve flipped to contango and every roll began to bleed. A cash-flow mismatch plus an adverse roll is the same pair that shows up in levered ETFs and futures carry today. Being right about the destination does not pay the calls you owe along the way.

cards.hook: Recall it: what does an ADHD brain fail to feel, not fight?
cards.body: Take a beat before the answer lands. The deficit is not laziness or thin discipline. It is **interval timing**, the internal sense of how much time has actually gone by. Duration does not register, so a five-minute email eats an hour and a deadline three days out feels unreal. That is why trying harder does nothing. You cannot muscle a sense you do not have. The move is a prosthetic that puts time into your visual field, an analog timer with a shrinking wedge, a countdown on a second screen, a clock you actually glance at.
cards.depth: Retrieving this again matters because the failure keeps returning in fresh disguises. A build that runs long, a bedtime that slips, a call that overruns. Same missing gauge each time. Adding a timer does not train you to track time, it converts an invisible quantity into something the eyes can see and the broken internal clock cannot quietly hide.

cards.hook: A fat dividend can get your short call assigned early.
cards.body: American-style short calls face early exercise risk when a call's extrinsic value drops below the dividend the stock is about to pay. A holder who exercises the night before ex-date captures the dividend and forfeits only the now-cheap time value. It's not random: it clusters right before ex-dividend dates on deep ITM, low-IV calls. Assignment lands you short stock at the open, **owing the dividend to whoever exercised**. Check ex-div calendars before holding short calls into dividend-heavy names.
cards.depth: Deep ITM covered calls on dividend aristocrats are the classic trap: sell a call worth $0.50 of extrinsic value against a $0.60 dividend and assignment is nearly certain. Brokers don't warn you; you find out via an overnight position change. It's also why call open interest on dividend stocks drops sharply right before ex-date, as short sellers who understand the math close out first.

cards.hook: Only two levers reliably open your starting gate.
cards.body: ADHD task initiation runs on an interest-based nervous system, not an importance-based one. Deadlines and stakes don't reliably trigger the dopamine needed to start; **novelty and urgency do**. That's why a task due in three weeks sits untouched, then gets finished in the last two hours. The three-week version has no urgency signal yet. Manufacture one: fake deadlines, timers, public commitments, or breaking work into a five-minute first step reframes 'important' into something your brain will act on now.
cards.depth: This isn't a willpower gap, it's a difference in what counts as a starting signal. Importance gets evaluated consciously; urgency and novelty trigger dopamine more directly and involuntarily. Body doubling and hard deadlines work for the same reason: they import urgency from outside instead of waiting for it to build on its own.

cards.hook: Outside view beats inside view for time estimates.
cards.body: The inside view estimates a task by reasoning through its specific steps: what has to happen, in what order, how long each piece takes. It reliably underestimates, because it can't account for what you haven't anticipated yet. The **outside view** asks a different question: how long did similar projects actually take, ignoring this one's details. Kahneman calls this reference-class forecasting. It's uncomfortable because it throws away information that feels relevant, and accurate because that's exactly what makes every planner overconfident.
cards.depth: Flyvbjerg's research on infrastructure megaprojects found this pattern at scale: planners reasoning from their own project's specifics were consistently more wrong than planners who simply asked what similar projects historically took. The fix isn't sharper inside reasoning, it's finding your reference class first and anchoring there before you build the detailed estimate.

cards.hook: Fair training and legal copies are different questions.
cards.body: Courts are increasingly splitting AI training cases into two separate questions: whether training on copyrighted text is fair use, and whether the copies used to train were obtained legally. In the major recent rulings, judges found the training itself transformative and likely fair, while treating **downloading from pirate shadow libraries** as a separate, unprotected act carrying its own liability. Practitioners keep arguing the fair-use question and forgetting the acquisition question, but a client can lose entirely on the second even after winning the first.
cards.depth: This split matters for deal drafting: a warranty promising only 'lawfully trained data' isn't enough anymore. The stronger clause requires the vendor to warrant its training corpus was lawfully acquired, not just fairly used, since courts now treat those as separate exposures they analyze one at a time.

cards.hook: Recall it: why does a warm bath before bed help sleep?
cards.body: Your body temperature has to drop to initiate sleep, and a hot bath triggers a **bigger rebound cooling** than sitting still would. Blood vessels near your skin dilate to dump heat, so when you get out, your core temperature falls faster and further than it would have on its own. That drop is one of the signals your circadian system reads as 'sleep window open.' Timing matters: the effect needs roughly an hour to unfold, so a bath right at lights-out is too late to catch the cooling curve.
cards.depth: This is why a cold plunge right before bed can backfire: it triggers a stress-hormone spike that can override the cooling benefit. The bath needs to be hot enough to dilate vessels, not so cold it activates a fight-or-flight response instead.

cards.hook: Your delta hedge drifts overnight even when nothing moves.
cards.body: Charm is the rate at which delta changes as time passes, holding spot fixed. As expiration nears, an in-the-money option's delta drifts toward 1 and an out-of-the-money option's toward 0. So a book that was delta-neutral at Friday's close can open Monday off-neutral purely from the weekend passing, before a single tick. **Charm is largest for near-the-money options close to expiry**, which is exactly where most premium-sellers live. Rehedging at Monday's open isn't reacting to news; it's paying down drift that time already baked in.
cards.depth: The effect concentrates around weekends and holidays, because three or more calendar days of decay accrue against only two trading sessions of hedging opportunity. Desks that mark charm explicitly pre-position on Friday rather than chase their own delta into the Monday auction.

cards.hook: Copying an artist's style isn't infringement. Copying their expression is.
cards.body: Copyright protects specific expression, not style, technique, or genre. An image model trained to paint 'in the style of' a living artist generally does not infringe on that basis alone, because style is an unprotectable idea. Liability turns on whether an **output is substantially similar to a specific protected work**, or whether the training copies themselves were unlawful. That's why the strongest plaintiff theories in the art cases attack the ingestion step and near-duplicate outputs, not the vibe. A lawyer promising a client 'style protection' is selling something the Copyright Act does not grant.
cards.depth: Right of publicity can sometimes reach where copyright can't, when mimicry evokes a specific identifiable person for commercial gain. But that's an identity claim, not a copyright one, and it varies sharply by state. Conflating the two is the common practitioner error.

cards.hook: Switching tasks leaves part of your attention stuck behind.
cards.body: Attention residue, from Sophie Leroy's 2009 research, is the finding that when you switch from one task to another, part of your attention stays snagged on the first. Performance on the new task suffers until the residue clears. Everyone has this, but weaker inhibition means you snag more easily and clear more slowly. So the real cost of a 'quick' email check mid-deal isn't the two minutes; it's the **degraded focus you carry into the next hour**. The fix is structural, not disciplinary: batch similar tasks and finish a sub-unit before switching, so the loop closes instead of lingering.
cards.depth: This is also why an interrupt-heavy environment punishes ADHD disproportionately. Each interruption plants fresh residue, and the recovery tax is paid by the executive-function system that's already the bottleneck. Killing notifications isn't hygiene theater; it removes the residue source at the point of entry.

cards.hook: One trader's gas bet erased $6 billion in a week.
cards.body: In September 2006, Amaranth Advisors, a multistrategy fund, lost roughly $6.6 billion, most of it on natural-gas calendar spreads run by one trader, Brian Hunter. He was long winter and short shoulder-season contracts in size so large he had effectively become the market in those spreads. When the spread turned against him, there was **no one to sell to but himself**, and his own exit pressure drove the loss deeper. The lesson isn't that the bet was insane; parts of it were defensible. It's that a position you can't exit without moving the price isn't a position, it's a trap.
cards.depth: Concentration risk and liquidity risk are the same risk wearing two names. Position size relative to daily volume is the number that predicts whether you control the trade or it controls you. Amaranth's book was a multiple of the open interest that could realistically clear.

cards.hook: Recall it: how often is your 90% range actually right?
cards.body: Give yourself a beat before the answer. You set a range you're 90% sure contains the true value. The calibration studies put the real hit rate closer to **40 to 50%**, not 90. The interval comes out too narrow because you anchor on your best guess and adjust too little. The tell is surprise: if reality keeps landing outside your bounds, the bounds are lying to you.
cards.depth: Why it matters again: every position size and every deal forecast rides on an implied confidence interval. If yours run half as wide as they should, you're systematically underpricing the odds you're wrong, which is the exact error that blows up a book. Widen until it feels slightly ridiculous.

cards.hook: A strike gets touched twice as often as it finishes there.
cards.body: For a roughly driftless underlying, the chance price *ever* trades through a strike before expiry is about **twice the chance it expires beyond that strike**. So a short put with a 20% chance of finishing in the money carries roughly a 40% chance of being tested intraday. That is the reflection principle: every path that ends back on the safe side had to cross the strike once to get there. It is why 'it'll probably expire fine' and 'I'll probably get a scary touch' are both true at the same time.
cards.depth: The 2x rule assumes no drift and continuous paths. Positive drift lowers put touches and raises call touches, and a fat-tailed real tape touches even more than the Gaussian says. Use it to budget how often you'll be tempted to roll, not as a fill probability.

cards.hook: Give on what you value least to win what you value most.
cards.body: When two sides rank the open issues differently, you can trade cheap-to-you concessions for expensive-to-them ones and both walk away better off. Researchers call it **logrolling**, and it is why splitting every issue down the middle is usually the worst available outcome: it leaves joint value on the table. The move is to bundle. 'I'll give you the credit and the announce date if you give me the audit right and the reversion.' Single-issue haggling can never find those trades, because it never lets either side reveal what it actually cares about.
cards.depth: It only works if you know your own ranking cold before the room. Walk in with issues sorted into give, trade, and hold. The counterparty's fight over a low-rank item is a gift: it tells you their currency, which is exactly what you buy the high-rank item with.

cards.hook: A 1970 rule made reruns a goldmine, then its repeal killed it.
cards.body: The FCC's **Financial Interest and Syndication Rules** barred the three networks from owning a stake in, or the reruns of, the shows they aired. Networks had to license programming from studios and hand back the syndication rights. That handed studios the back-end fortune when a hit went into reruns, and it kept content ownership separate from distribution. Repealed in 1993, it let networks own their shows again. The direct result was vertical re-integration and the wave of studio-network mergers that followed. A rule built to stop concentration, whose death enabled it.
cards.depth: The repeal is why a Disney can own ABC and the studio feeding it, or a network can greenlight only shows it will own forever. The old separation, whatever its flaws, was the last structural check on one company owning both the pipe and the water.

cards.hook: A hot bath before bed works by cooling you down.
cards.body: Sleep onset is triggered by a **fall in core body temperature**, roughly 1 degree C as you drift off. Warming your skin, especially hands and feet, opens the blood vessels there and dumps heat from the core, so warming the outside actually cools the inside. A pooled analysis of passive body-heating studies reported that a warm bath or shower one to two hours before bed sped up sleep onset by roughly ten minutes on average. The timing matters. Too close to bed and you are still shedding heat when you want to already be asleep.
cards.depth: This is also why a cool bedroom near 65 F helps, and why socks cut both ways: warm feet early aid the heat dump, but overheating under blankets stalls the core-temp drop the whole system depends on.

cards.hook: Models read the middle of a long prompt worst.
cards.body: Give a model a long context and its recall is U-shaped: it uses what sits at the **very start and the very end** far better than anything buried in the middle. Researchers named it 'lost in the middle,' and it holds even for models whose context window officially fits the whole document. So the fix is not a bigger window. Put the instruction and the single most important fact at the top or the bottom, never at 50% depth. When you paste ten files, the one that matters goes first or last, not fifth.
cards.depth: It falls out of how attention and training distribute weight, not a bug you can prompt away. Practical test: if an answer keeps ignoring a detail, move that detail to the edge of the prompt before you rewrite anything else.

cards.hook: The variance premium is a risk fee, not a mistake.
cards.body: You collect it because your short-vol position loses **in exactly the states that hurt most**: crashes, when every other asset is falling and a dollar is worth more to you. A rational buyer pays above fair value for that protection, and you earn the spread for bearing crash risk nobody else wants. This reframes the whole strategy. You are not exploiting an inefficiency that should arbitrage itself away, you are being paid a genuine risk premium for a real service. It also warns you: the premium is thinnest, and the danger largest, right after a calm stretch when insurance feels pointless.
cards.depth: The corollary is that no amount of edge sharpening removes the risk, because the return IS the risk compensation. Sizing, not cleverness, is the lever. A short-vol book that never has a bad quarter is almost certainly underpriced risk waiting to be repriced.

cards.hook: Pure AI images get no copyright. Your arrangement of them can.
cards.body: The Copyright Office refused protection for the Midjourney images in **Zarya of the Dawn** (2023), then registered the comic's human-written text and the selection, coordination, and arrangement of those images. Thaler v. Perlmutter confirmed the baseline in 2025: a work needs human authorship to register at all. The practical error is treating 'AI-generated' as one uncopyrightable blob. It is layered. The prompting, editing, sequencing, and compositing a human actually contributes can carry thin protection even when each raw output cannot, which changes how you paper ownership and chain-of-title in any AI-assisted production.
cards.depth: For clearance work this means two questions, not one: what did the model output, and what did a human do to it? The second answer is where any registrable interest lives, and it is worth documenting the human contribution contemporaneously rather than reconstructing it later.

cards.hook: A positive result on a rare-condition test is usually a false alarm.

cards.body: Take a condition 1% of people have and a test that is 90% accurate both ways. Screen 1,000 people: 10 are sick and 9 test positive; 990 are healthy and 99 test positive anyway. A positive result therefore carries only about a **9% chance of actually being sick**, even though the test is 90% accurate. Intuition screams 90%. The gap is base-rate neglect: you anchor on the test's accuracy and ignore how rare the thing is. Every rare-signal detector inherits this, from fraud flags to insider-trading alerts to security screens.
cards.depth: The operational lesson is that a low base rate makes most alarms false no matter how good the detector, so the fix is never a better test alone. Either raise the prior before testing, or require a second independent signal before you act on the first.

cards.hook: Recall it: why does moving your backtest's start date kill the edge?
cards.body: Give yourself a beat before the answer lands. You picked the sample boundaries after glancing at the data, so the default window quietly flatters the strategy. That is **start-date data snooping**. A real edge stays roughly stable when you slide the start and end dates or run rolling windows; a fragile one swings wildly or vanishes. The reported number was always just one draw from many possible histories. The fix is cheap: report the metric across dozens of overlapping windows and read the distribution, not the point estimate.
cards.depth: Why it matters again: any parameter or rule you chose while staring at the same data inherits this bias, not just the dates. An edge that survives only its own birthday was never an edge.

cards.hook: An unwritten to-do keeps evicting the task you're on.
cards.body: Working memory has a small, shared workspace, and ADHD shrinks it further. Every 'don't forget to call the CPA' you hold in your head **occupies the same register that's running your current task**. The intrusive thought does not wait politely; it competes, and often wins, which is why you lose the thread mid-draft. The move is to externalize on contact: one always-open capture note where the stray item goes the second it appears. You are not being organized. You are clearing the workspace so the single task in front of you keeps the whole register.
cards.depth: This is why 'I'll just remember it' fails specifically for you: the remembering itself consumes the exact resource the work needs. Offload the moment it surfaces, review the list on a fixed schedule, and stop paying rent on things a note could hold for free.

cards.hook: Half-Kelly isn't caution. It's paying for uncertainty.
cards.body: Full Kelly maximizes long-run growth only if you know your edge exactly. You never do. You estimate it from noisy history, and the estimate sits above the truth as often as below. Betting full Kelly on an inflated estimate is betting well past full Kelly on reality, where growth falls off a cliff. **Halving the fraction buys a wide margin against that estimation error** for only a small give-up in growth. Half-Kelly is not timidity. It is the honest price of not knowing your true edge.
cards.depth: The growth curve is nearly flat just under its peak and steep just past it, so overbetting hurts far more than underbetting the same distance. With fat-tailed short-vol returns, historical edge is especially overstated, which pushes the prudent fraction below even half.

cards.hook: Body doubling works by borrowing someone else's brakes.
cards.body: ADHD is an under-supply of inhibition: the internal brake that keeps a dull task from losing to a more interesting impulse is weak. Another person in the room supplies the brake from outside. Task-switching now carries a social cost, and 'I'll just check my phone' carries a witness. **The mechanism is borrowed inhibition, not motivation or shame.** That is why a silent, uninterested co-worker helps as much as an expert one, and why a scheduled call to just sit and work often out-performs any productivity app you could install instead.
cards.depth: Concrete move: book a standing 30-minute video call with anyone, cameras on, no agenda beyond each of you doing your own work. The presence does the work. Solo fallback: a livestream or a busy cafe supplies a weaker version of the same external brake.

cards.hook: Anthropic won on fair use and still paid $1.5 billion.
cards.body: In June 2025 a federal judge ruled that training a model on books was transformative fair use. Anthropic still faced a reported $1.5 billion settlement. The reason is the split the court drew: **learning from a work is fair use, but how you got the copy is a separate act.** Anthropic had downloaded pirated libraries to assemble its corpus, and piracy is infringement no matter what you later do with the files. The lesson for any AI builder is that clean acquisition, not the training step, is where the liability now lives.
cards.depth: Contrast the Meta ruling weeks later, where training also cleared fair use but the plaintiffs lost mainly on a thin market-harm record. Two wins for AI on the training question, and the surviving exposure in both is sourcing and market-dilution proof, not the model itself.

cards.hook: Your best estimate ignores every time you ran late before.
cards.body: Asked how long something will take, you build a story: the steps, the good days, the clean run. That inside view is why nearly every plan runs late. The fix is not more detail. It is to set your own case aside and ask what actually happened to similar projects, then use that spread of outcomes as your starting number. **Reference-class forecasting beats introspection because your imagined steps are optimistic and the base rate already prices in the surprises.** Kahneman found that even experts, handed the base rate, still trusted their own narrative and blew the estimate.
cards.depth: Practical version: before estimating a build, pull three past builds of the same shape and take their real elapsed time, not the version you remember. Anchor on that, then adjust for genuine differences. Keep the adjustment small; if it grows large, you have slid back into the inside view.

cards.hook: Recall it: whose 1944 suit freed actors after seven years?
cards.body: About ten days back: one 1944 lawsuit set a hard ceiling on how long a studio could bind a performer. Which star, and what was the ceiling? Take a second before the reveal. **It was Olivia de Havilland, and the ceiling was seven calendar years.** She sued Warner Bros. over the trick of tacking suspensions onto the end of a contract to stretch it indefinitely, and won. California's seven-year statute has been the De Havilland Law ever since, and it still shapes how long talent can be locked up.
cards.depth: The rule runs seven years from the start of actual service, not seven years of work performed, which is exactly why suspension-stacking was the whole fight. Recording artists later won a controversial carve-out, but the baseline ceiling still traces to her case.

cards.hook: Implied vol beats realized vol most months. That's your paycheck.
cards.body: On the S&P index, option-implied volatility has historically run a few points above the volatility that later shows up, on average, reported around 3 to 4 vol points. That gap is the **variance risk premium**, the compensation sellers earn for warehousing crash risk. It is not a mispricing you outsmart; it is insurance buyers knowingly overpay for because they hate the tail. The premium is fattest and steadiest in the index, thinner in single names, and it inverts violently in a crisis when realized vol blows past implied.
cards.depth: The carry is real but the payoff profile is short a lottery ticket. Selling index vol is also short correlation and short the tail, so the losing days cluster together instead of arriving one at a time.

cards.hook: The first 'training isn't fair use' win involved no generative AI.
cards.body: In Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence (Delaware, February 2025), the court held that using Westlaw's headnotes to train a competing legal-research tool was not fair use. The twist practitioners miss: **Ross's AI was not generative.** It did not write anything; it retrieved relevant case law. The judge leaned hard on the fourth factor, market harm, because Ross built a direct substitute for Westlaw. Generative defendants keep citing transformative-use wins, but this ruling says substitution can swamp transformation once the output competes commercially with its source.
cards.depth: The generative fair-use wins turned partly on outputs being non-substitutive for the originals. Ross shows the fourth factor doing the heavy lifting: a model that competes with the thing it trained on is exposed no matter how transformative the ingestion looks.

cards.hook: You can't feel time passing, so make it visible.
cards.body: ADHD carries a measurable deficit in **interval timing**, the internal sense of how long something has taken. Duration does not register, so a 'quick email' eats an hour and a deadline three days out feels like it does not exist yet. The fix is not discipline, it is a prosthetic: put elapsed and remaining time into your visual field where a broken internal clock cannot hide it. An analog timer showing a shrinking wedge, a countdown on a second screen, a clock you actually glance at. You are not tracking time better, you are turning it into a thing the eyes can see.
cards.depth: This is the same move as writing your to-do list down instead of holding it in your head. The intervention pattern for ADHD is consistent: take a weak internal function and offload it onto an external surface the environment maintains for you.

cards.hook: When you disagree about the future, bet on it in the contract.
cards.body: Deals often stall because the two sides forecast differently: seller swears the numbers will hit, buyer doubts it. Splitting the difference leaves both feeling robbed. The cleaner move is a **contingent contract**, a term that pays out based on which forecast comes true, an earnout, a milestone bonus, a clawback. Each side gets to bet on its own optimism instead of arguing it. It doubles as a lie detector: the party that refuses to tie money to its own confident prediction is telling you the prediction was cheap talk.
cards.depth: The trigger has to be clean, measurable, and hard to game, with a defined window, or you have just moved the fight from price to accounting. Earnouts breed litigation exactly when the metric is squishy or the buyer controls the levers that drive it.

cards.hook: Recall it: which side of your reference point makes you a gambler?
cards.body: A hint: it is the same asymmetry that makes you bank a winner too early and ride a loser too long. Take a beat before it lands. Prospect theory found people are **risk-averse over gains but risk-seeking over losses.** A sure $100 gain beats a coin flip for $200, but a sure $100 loss loses to that same flip, even though the odds are identical. The distortion lives around your entry price, not the real probabilities. Below the reference point, a certain loss feels unbearable and the gamble feels like rescue.
cards.depth: Your reference point is arbitrary, usually just the price you paid, and the market has no idea it exists. Every 'let me get back to flat' is that arbitrary anchor quietly overriding expected value.

cards.hook: In a selloff your delta moves faster than gamma predicts.
cards.body: Gamma tells you how delta changes as spot moves. But delta also shifts as implied vol moves, and vol usually spikes when spot drops. That cross-sensitivity is **vanna**. For a short put, falling spot plus rising vol drives delta more negative than gamma alone predicts, so a hedge sized on gamma comes up short exactly when the move is violent. Dealers hedging their own vanna sell more futures into the drop, which feeds the slide you were trying to hedge against.
cards.depth: Vanna is largest for out-of-the-money options with time left. It is why a book that looks delta-neutral at Friday's vol can be quietly long risk if Monday gaps down. Rehedge to realized conditions, not the vol you booked.

cards.hook: Tennessee made distributing a voice-clone tool itself illegal.
cards.body: The ELVIS Act, effective July 2024, added voice to Tennessee's right of publicity and did something unusual: it reaches the **toolmakers**. Liability is not limited to the person who deepfakes a singer. It extends to anyone who makes available a product or service whose primary purpose is producing an unauthorized clone of a real voice. Most publicity statutes target the end use. Tennessee moved the target upstream to the software itself, which is why platform lawyers now read it more closely than the flashier California statutes.
cards.depth: The right is descendible, so it survives the performer's death. The open question practitioners flag is how primary purpose applies to a general-purpose model that can clone a voice among a thousand other tasks.

cards.hook: Your 90% confidence range is right about half the time.
cards.body: Ask people for a range they are 90% sure contains an answer, and the true value lands outside it far more than 10% of the time. Classic calibration studies put actual hit rates near 40 to 50%. The interval is too narrow because you anchor on your best guess and adjust too little. **Surprise is the tell:** if reality keeps landing outside your ranges, the ranges are lying. Two fixes that work: set the bounds by assuming you are already wrong and asking why, then widen until it feels slightly ridiculous.
cards.depth: This is why position sizing and litigation-outcome estimates both drift optimistic. The disciplined move is a range wide enough that being wrong would genuinely shock you, treated as your real uncertainty rather than the tight number you first felt.

cards.hook: Hyperfocus is a broken brake, not a strong engine.
cards.body: The same weak inhibition that makes starting hard also makes stopping hard. Hyperfocus is not extra focus; it is a **failure to disengage**, driven by the same executive-function gap. That is why you can surface from a build at 6 PM with no sense of the hours passing. Willpower will not generate the stop signal, because the machinery that produces stop signals is the part that is impaired. The fix has to be external: a loud alarm set before you enter, not a mental note to check the time.
cards.depth: Stack it so the interrupt forces a physical action, standing up or leaving the room, because an alarm you can silence from your chair gets silenced and ignored. For a 5:00 pickup, the alarm goes at 4:30 and lives across the room.

cards.hook: Recall it: does a precise or round opening offer anchor harder?
cards.body: A few days back: two opening offers, one round at $500,000 and one precise at $512,000. Which pulls the final number further toward it? **The precise one.** Round figures signal a rough guess and invite large counter-swings. A specific figure signals you ran the math, so counterparties adjust in smaller increments and settle closer to your anchor. The move: open precise rather than round, and open first when you actually know the range.
cards.depth: The effect shows up in home-price and salary studies, where precise asks correlate with final prices nearer the ask. The caveat: precision must stay plausible. A number that looks arbitrarily exact reads as gamesmanship and burns the credibility that made precision work.

cards.hook: Dealers long gamma quietly trade against every move you make.
cards.body: When market makers are net long gamma, staying delta-neutral forces them to sell into rallies and buy into dips. That mechanical flow **dampens realized volatility** and pins price toward large open-interest strikes, especially into a monthly expiration. Flip the sign, dealers net short gamma, and the same hedging runs with the move: they buy higher and sell lower, feeding trend and expansion. The regime isn't cosmetic. It decides whether mean-reversion or momentum is the better short-horizon bet, and it's estimable from options open interest and spot's distance from the peak-gamma strike.
cards.depth: The caveat: gamma-exposure estimates depend on guessing who is long versus short each strike, and public GEX figures infer that split from open interest alone. Treat the sign and rough magnitude as signal. Treat any precise flip level as a fitted number that can be wrong on the day you most want it.

cards.hook: California now needs a dead performer's estate to say yes.
cards.body: AB 1836, effective January 2025, bars producing or distributing a **digital replica of a deceased performer** in new work without the estate's consent. It sits beside California's older postmortem right of publicity in Civil Code 3344.1, but it's narrower and sharper: it targets AI-generated performances specifically, reaches expressive works the older statute often exempted, and runs 70 years past death. The practical shift for anyone clearing archival or synthetic-revival projects is that a public-domain film clip and a newly generated performance of the same late actor now sit under genuinely different rules.
cards.depth: The consent requirement carries carve-outs for news, documentary, satire, commentary, and some biographical or historical uses, mirroring First Amendment limits already litigated under the right of publicity. Expect the real fights there, at the seam between a licensed synthetic performance and a protected expressive one. That seam is where the statute's edges get drawn.

cards.hook: Pre-decide the trigger, and starting stops needing willpower.
cards.body: Implementation intentions are if-then plans: 'if it's 9am and I've sat down, then I open the brief.' In Gollwitzer's research they reliably beat plain goal intentions, and the gap is **largest for people with weak self-regulation**, which is the ADHD case exactly. The mechanism is delegation: you hand the start decision to a specific environmental cue, so initiation fires on the cue instead of demanding executive control you can't summon on command. A vague goal ('work on the deal today') leaves the trigger unspecified, so the brain never gets a signal. Name the cue and the first physical action, once, in advance.
cards.depth: Keep the 'then' a single concrete act, not a project: 'open the file,' not 'write the memo.' The cue should be something that happens whether or not you intend it, a clock time, finishing coffee, sitting at the desk. The plan works precisely because it rides a moment that was going to arrive anyway.

cards.hook: Slide the start date six months and watch the edge die.
cards.body: A backtest reports one number, but it's one draw from many possible histories. Shift the start and end dates by a few months, or run rolling windows, and a genuine edge stays roughly stable while a fragile one swings wildly or vanishes. The trap: you almost always pick the boundaries after glancing at the data, so the default sample quietly flatters the strategy, a form of **start-date data snooping**. The fix is cheap. Report the metric across dozens of overlapping windows and read the distribution, not the point estimate. An edge that survives only its own birthday was never an edge.
cards.depth: This is the walk-forward instinct applied to sample boundaries instead of parameters. Same principle: never let one arbitrary choice, a start date, a parameter, a universe, carry the whole result. If the conclusion flips when you nudge any single one of them, the conclusion was the noise, not the signal you were hunting.

cards.hook: Recall it: a formula beat the experts using what weights?
cards.body: Think back to Meehl and Dawes. The experts were good at one half of the job and reliably bad at the other half. Which half, and what beat them? The answer: models with **unit weights**, just standardize the factors and add them, no fitted coefficients, matched or beat the experts who chose those very factors. Experts know which variables matter; they simply can't combine them the same way twice. A formula combines identically every time, stripping out the noise in the human head. The move for any repeated call: pick the factors once, weight them equally, tally.
cards.depth: Where it bites for you: sizing a position, ranking a hire, deciding whether to settle. The pull is always to 'weigh it all holistically,' and that holistic step is exactly the noisy one. Name three or four factors in advance, score each, add them, and let the sum argue with your gut before you override it.

cards.hook: The straddle price is the expected move, not one sigma.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="360" y2="200" stroke="#35302a"/><rect x="120" y="72" width="60" height="128" fill="none" stroke="#d9a441"/><rect x="250" y="40" width="60" height="160" fill="none" stroke="#7fb4a2"/><text x="150" y="220" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">straddle =</text><text x="150" y="236" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">expected move</text><text x="280" y="220" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">1 sigma</text><text x="280" y="30" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">~25% higher</text></svg>
cards.body: The at-the-money straddle costs roughly 0.8 x S x sigma x sqrt(T). That number also equals the expected absolute move of a normal variable, sigma x sqrt(T) x sqrt(2/pi), which is about 0.8 sigma. So buying the straddle pays the **mean absolute move**, not the 68% one-sigma band. The common error is to read the straddle as a one-sigma range and size trades off it, which overstates how often you land inside. The true one-sigma level sits roughly 25% above the straddle price.
cards.depth: Rule of thumb: the expected move is about the straddle price, while the one-sigma move is the straddle divided by 0.8. Traders who quote a single 'expected move' number are usually citing the first and treating it as the second.

cards.hook: Trials inflate your Sharpe. Deflate it before you believe it.
cards.body: Run enough strategy variants and the best Sharpe is partly luck dressed as signal. The **deflated Sharpe ratio** (Bailey and Lopez de Prado) discounts the observed number for how many trials you ran, how long the track record is, and the skew and fat tails of the returns. The more configurations you tried, the higher a Sharpe must clear to stay real. A 1.5 from one honest test can outrank a 2.5 mined from five hundred. If you cannot state the trial count, the number is theater.
cards.depth: The correction rises with the spread of your trial Sharpes and with the count of trials. It also punishes short samples and negative skew, since a smooth-looking equity curve can hide a rare blowup that a raw Sharpe quietly ignores.

cards.hook: Denmark wants to give you copyright in your own face.
cards.body: In 2025 Denmark's culture ministry proposed amending copyright law to give every person **rights over their own body, facial features, and voice**, so a realistic deepfake could be treated as infringement a platform must take down. That is a different engine from the US route, which pushes deepfakes through right-of-publicity and a patchwork of state statutes. Copyright carries built-in takedown machinery and cross-border treaties that publicity rights lack. Whether courts accept that your face is a protectable work is the open question, but the framing is the move to watch.
cards.depth: Reported as a proposal, not yet enacted. The interesting wrinkle for a practitioner: a copyright theory travels through the DMCA-style notice regimes and the Berne treaty network, so a Danish right could reach content hosted abroad in ways a purely state publicity claim never could.

cards.hook: Stop mid-sentence so tomorrow's start is already loaded.
cards.body: The costly part of a task is not the doing, it is the **activation threshold** to begin. A blank page hands the job to your weakest function, initiation, and asks it to make the first move from nothing. So do not finish clean. Stop with the next action half-done and obvious: a sentence trailing off, a test written but not yet run, the file open at the exact line. Re-entry then costs almost nothing, because the first move is already decided and visible. You spend good-state minutes to buy your bad-state self a running start.
cards.depth: This is why 'write the next step down before you quit' beats a tidy stopping point. You are not saving the work, you are lowering the energy needed to reopen it, which is the exact barrier initiation struggles with.

cards.hook: Recall it: your bet lost. Was the decision wrong?
cards.body: From a card a week or so back: **decision quality and outcome quality are separate** axes. You can take the positive-EV side and still lose, because variance gets a vote. Grading the decision by the result is resulting, and it quietly trains you to drop good process after an unlucky streak and to repeat reckless bets that happened to pay. Judge the call on what you knew and the odds you faced, not on where the ball landed. Log the reasoning at the time, so a bad result cannot rewrite the decision after the fact.

cards.hook: Near the strike at the close, you can't know your position.
cards.body: A short option sitting right at its strike into the close creates **pin risk**: you cannot tell whether it finishes a penny in or out, so you don't know if you'll be assigned. You find out after the bell, sometimes hours later, by which point the underlying has moved in after-hours or gapped over the weekend. What looked like a flat, expiring position hands you unhedged stock Monday morning. The fix is to close anything hovering near the strike before expiration rather than gamble on where it prints.
cards.depth: Clearing firms auto-exercise anything ITM by $0.01 under exercise-by-exception, but a counterparty can file contrary instructions, or decline. So even a clearly ITM short can go unassigned, and a near-money one is a coin flip whose result you learn too late to hedge.

cards.hook: Your backtest shorted stocks nobody would actually lend you.
cards.body: Backtests silently assume every short is available, free, and infinite. Reality: hard-to-borrow names carry **borrow fees** that can run from a few percent to well over 50% annualized, and sometimes the shares simply aren't there to lend. The cruel part is selection. The fattest short-side signals (overpriced meme names, fresh IPOs, distressed tickers) cluster in exactly the stocks that are expensive or impossible to short. A strategy that looks brilliant long-short can be uninvestable on the short leg once real borrow costs and availability hit.
cards.depth: The tell is a long-short backtest whose entire edge lives in the short book. Re-run it long-only, or charge a punitive borrow to the hardest names, and watch how much Sharpe was really just an assumption about lending.

cards.hook: A vague digital-replica clause is now void in California.
cards.body: California's AB 2602, effective January 1, 2025, makes a contract term allowing use of a performer's **digital replica** unenforceable when the replica would substitute for work they'd otherwise do in person, unless the intended use is described with reasonable specificity or the performer was represented by a lawyer or union. The old catch-all grant, replica rights across 'all media now known or hereafter devised,' no longer binds an unrepresented actor. Specificity, not breadth, is what now makes the clause hold.
cards.depth: It pairs with AB 1836, which requires estate consent to use a deceased performer's digital replica in expressive works. Together they push replica rights from a boilerplate land-grab toward use-by-use consent, and they reward having counsel or a guild in the room.

cards.hook: In the red, you quietly turn into a gambler.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><line x1="40" y1="120" x2="380" y2="120" stroke="#35302a"/><line x1="200" y1="30" x2="200" y2="215" stroke="#35302a"/><path d="M200,120 Q280,62 375,55" fill="none" stroke="#d9a441" stroke-width="2.5"/><path d="M200,120 Q128,178 45,214" fill="none" stroke="#d9a441" stroke-width="2.5"/><text x="288" y="46" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14">gains: flatter</text><text x="58" y="206" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14">losses: steeper</text><text x="206" y="26" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13">reference point</text></svg>
cards.body: Prospect theory found a clean asymmetry: people are **risk-averse over gains but risk-seeking over losses**. Offered a sure $100 versus a coin flip for $200 or nothing, most take the sure thing. Flip the signs, a sure $100 loss versus a coin flip to lose $200 or nothing, and most gamble, even though the expected value is identical or worse. It's why a trader banks winners early and holds losers hoping to get back to flat. The distortion lives around your reference point, the price you got in, not the actual odds.
cards.depth: The reference point is the lever. Reframe the loser as a fresh position you'd have to actively buy today at the current price, and the urge to gamble your way back to even usually dies. You wouldn't open it now; you're only holding because of where you started.

cards.hook: Distant payoffs feel worthless. Bolt on a near one.
cards.body: ADHD steepens **delay discounting**: a reward a week out is marked down so hard it barely pulls you, while the same reward now works fine. So the move isn't willpower, it's manufacturing a near-term payoff for a task whose real payoff is too distant to motivate. The coffee only gets made while the filing goes out. The podcast only plays during the admin block. You're not treating yourself. You're bolting an immediate consequence onto work whose actual consequence sits too far away to reach you.
cards.depth: This is temptation bundling with a mechanism attached. It fails when the reward is available with or without the task, so the pairing has to be exclusive: the near-term thing you want is gated behind the thing you're avoiding, or the bridge doesn't hold.

cards.hook: Your SPX monthly settles on prints you never get to trade.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><line x1="30" y1="150" x2="370" y2="150" stroke="#35302a" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="90" y1="143" x2="90" y2="157" stroke="#7fb4a2" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="310" y1="143" x2="310" y2="157" stroke="#d9a441" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M90 118 v-8 h220 v8" fill="none" stroke="#d9a441" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="200" y="95" text-anchor="middle" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14">16+ hours: gap risk you cannot hedge</text><text x="90" y="176" text-anchor="middle" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13">Thu 4:00 ET</text><text x="90" y="193" text-anchor="middle" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13">last trade</text><text x="310" y="176" text-anchor="middle" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13">Fri open</text><text x="310" y="193" text-anchor="middle" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13">SET prints</text></svg>
cards.body: The traditional third-Friday SPX contract stops trading Thursday afternoon, but its settlement value, SET, is computed from Friday's opening print of each constituent stock. For sixteen-plus hours you hold a position whose final value is not yet set and cannot be traded. Overnight news gaps it, and because the 500 stocks open at staggered times, SET routinely lands away from the index's quoted Friday open - it is a synthetic price no ticker ever displayed. **You carry gap risk you can no longer hedge.** PM-settled Weeklys and end-of-month series exist precisely to remove this window; know which series you sold.
cards.depth: The window is not hypothetical: major economic releases land Friday mornings, inside it. Wings that looked safely OTM at Thursday's close can settle in the money on the open. Cash settlement means no assignment machinery softens it - just a debit at a price you watched happen, flat-footed.

cards.hook: Your backtest fills at mid. The market never will.
cards.body: Most options backtests mark every entry and exit at the bid-ask midpoint. Live, you surrender part of the spread on every leg, every side, every roll - and in far OTM wings the spread can be a double-digit percentage of the premium itself. A strategy collecting small credits across four legs pays that toll eight times per round trip, more with adjustments. So re-run the test assuming fills a fixed fraction of the way toward the far side, and watch what survives. **An edge thinner than the spread give-up never existed** - the backtest was measuring a price nobody offers.
cards.depth: The second-order problem: spreads widen exactly when volatility spikes, so execution costs correlate with your strategy's worst moments. A constant slippage haircut still understates crisis-period costs. If the strategy's P&L concentrates in high-vol regimes, model slippage as a function of vol, not a constant.

cards.hook: Apple's e-book MFN did the price-fixing by itself.
cards.body: In 2010 Apple entered e-books with agency contracts carrying a retail-price MFN: if any retailer sold a title cheaper, Apple could match. Apple never told publishers to move Amazon off $9.99. It didn't have to. Under agency-plus-MFN, any publisher that left Amazon at $9.99 would watch Apple match it and eat the margin on every iBooks sale - so the five majors forced Amazon onto agency within months, and prices jumped to $12.99 and $14.99. The court treated the MFN as the engine of the conspiracy. **The clause outsourced enforcement to the counterparties' own incentives.** Draft MFNs knowing they act at a distance.
cards.depth: United States v. Apple (S.D.N.Y. 2013, affirmed 2d Cir. 2015). The general lesson for any deal: an MFN is not passive protection. It changes what your counterparty must do in negotiations you are not part of - which is sometimes the point, and sometimes the liability.

cards.hook: Automate where checking is cheap, not where doing is hard.
cards.body: The question that decides whether an agent helps isn't 'can the model do this?' It's 'what does verifying the output cost me?' Code with a test suite verifies mechanically, so generation can be mediocre and retry until green. A one-shot client email verifies only through the same judgment that could have written it, so delegation saves nothing and adds a review pass. The working rule: **build the verifier before the generator** - a schema, a test, an artifact you can measure. Where a cheap verifier exists, models scale. Where it doesn't, every output lands back in your attention, which was the scarce resource all along.
cards.depth: This is why structured-output schemas and self-check scripts buy more than prompt wording: they convert an open-ended judgment call into a pass/fail gate. It is also why 'human in the loop' plans quietly stall - the loop is unbudgeted verification, and it accumulates.

cards.hook: Recall it: why could Seinfeld money never happen again?
cards.body: Before you look: it was a regulation, it lasted a quarter century, and its repeal remade the industry within a decade. Got it? The fin-syn rules (1970 to 1995) barred ABC, CBS and NBC from owning or syndicating their prime-time shows, forcing them to rent from studios and independents - which left producers holding the backend that built the Cosby and Seinfeld fortunes. Repeal let the buyer own the show: Disney bought ABC within months, every network moved inside a studio, and **the cost-plus buyout is fin-syn's repeal completed** - the buyer owns everything, so nothing is left to syndicate.
cards.depth: Why it matters again: every streamer term you've negotiated - premium-over-cost, vanishing participations - is downstream of one FCC docket. When you argue backend today, you are arguing against ownership structure, not accounting. Structure beats formula every time.

cards.hook: Every index option carries a hidden correlation bet.
cards.body: An index can't move unless its components move together, so index variance is component variances glued by pairwise correlation. That means index implied vol embeds an implied correlation, and historically it has traded above what later gets realized - the **correlation risk premium**. The flow story: institutions buy index puts as macro hedges while call overwriting supplies single-name vol, so the index leg stays structurally rich. Dispersion desks harvest the gap - short index vol, long single-name vol, roughly vega-neutral. The catch rhymes with all vol selling: in a crash, correlations lurch toward 1 and the premium you collected goes out the door at once.
cards.depth: Rough magnitudes: S&P 500 implied correlation has run above realized by reported gaps of roughly 5-15 points depending on window and method. You can't run true dispersion retail - too many legs - but the concept still prices your book: selling index premium means you're short correlation whether you meant to be or not.

cards.hook: A formula with made-up weights still beats the expert.
cards.body: Paul Meehl showed in 1954 that simple statistical rules match or beat expert judgment in most prediction tasks, and decades of follow-up studies kept confirming it. Robyn Dawes pushed it further: models with **unit weights** - just add the standardized factors, no fitted coefficients - still beat the experts who picked the factors. The mechanism is noise, not knowledge. Experts are genuinely good at knowing which variables matter and reliably bad at combining them the same way twice; a formula combines identically every time. The move for any repeated call - hire, settle, size a position: name the handful of factors once, weight them equally, and let the tally argue with your gut.
cards.depth: Grove's meta-analysis of over 130 comparisons found mechanical prediction equaled or beat clinical judgment in the large majority of studies. Dawes' 1979 paper is 'The Robust Beauty of Improper Linear Models.' Same root as noise audits: two experts, same file, different answers - a formula never disagrees with itself.

cards.hook: Meta won its training case; the judge wrote plaintiffs a roadmap.
cards.body: In June 2025 Judge Chhabria granted Meta summary judgment: training Llama on the plaintiff authors' books was fair use. Then he spent much of the opinion explaining why that outcome should comfort no AI company. These plaintiffs simply failed to build a record on the theory that could win: **market dilution** - generative models flooding the market with works that compete with the books they trained on, depressing demand without copying any single one. Lost licensing revenue, the theory plaintiffs actually ran, he found circular and weak. Read alongside Alsup's Bartz ruling the same week, the message isn't 'training is legal.' It's 'plead the fourth factor correctly.'
cards.depth: The fourth fair-use factor - effect on the market for the original - has historically been the heavyweight. Chhabria's dilution theory needs no showing that any output copies a specific work; the harm is category-level substitution. Expect the next wave of complaints to arrive with economists attached.

cards.hook: The late-afternoon crash is pharmacology, not relapse.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 240' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><line x1='40' y1='210' x2='380' y2='210' stroke='#35302a' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='40' y1='20' x2='40' y2='210' stroke='#35302a' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M40 205 C 80 60, 120 45, 170 55 C 220 65, 260 120, 330 200' fill='none' stroke='#d9a441' stroke-width='3'/><line x1='262' y1='34' x2='262' y2='210' stroke='#7fb4a2' stroke-dasharray='4 4'/><line x1='334' y1='34' x2='334' y2='210' stroke='#7fb4a2' stroke-dasharray='4 4'/><text x='298' y='50' fill='#7fb4a2' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle'>rebound</text><text x='298' y='66' fill='#7fb4a2' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle'>window</text><text x='52' y='38' fill='#a89f8d' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='13'>blood level</text><text x='376' y='230' fill='#a89f8d' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='13' text-anchor='end'>hours after dose</text><text x='120' y='150' fill='#a89f8d' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='13'>smooth coverage</text></svg>
cards.body: As a stimulant's blood level falls, symptoms don't just come back - for an hour or so they can overshoot baseline, leaving focus and irritability worse than an unmedicated afternoon. That's **rebound**, a known crash on the falling edge of the concentration curve, not evidence the medication is failing. On lisdexamfetamine the fade typically starts 10-12 hours after the dose, which parks the window in the early evening. Two moves: schedule around it - mechanical, low-friction tasks in that slot, nothing that needs patience you won't have - and log the clock time the drop hits for a week. Offset timing is precisely the data that steers titration.
cards.depth: Rebound is distinct from tolerance (a weeks-scale question) and from peak-hours symptoms (a dose question). If the crash is severe or arrives early, prescribers commonly shift dose or timing - a conversation to bring data to. The diagram's window is schematic; your curve's actual timing is the thing worth measuring.

cards.hook: Conversational turns build language. Word count mostly doesn't.
cards.body: The famous '30-million-word gap' study tracked 42 families, and its headline number has not held up well under replication. What has held up is turn-taking. In a 2018 MIT study, the number of back-and-forth conversational exchanges predicted children's language scores and activation in Broca's area - **independent of word count and family income**. The mechanism looks like contingency: a response tuned to what the child just said or did gives the brain feedback it can learn from; narration aimed in their direction doesn't. For a 1-year-old that means treating babble as a serve to return. Answer it, pause, let them go again - the turn, not the monologue, is what the data rewards.
cards.depth: Romeo et al., Psychological Science 2018, ages 4-6; the imaging sample was small, so treat the neural finding as suggestive and the behavioral one as the anchor. Hart & Risley wasn't fabricated - it was underpowered and its framing overreached. Serve-and-return holds up across both literatures.

cards.hook: Recall it: who already got paid for the weekend's theta?
cards.body: It's Friday afternoon and you short premium to harvest three days of decay while the market sleeps. Before the reveal: who already ate that lunch, and when? Hold the question a beat. The answer: market makers, into Friday's close. They mark implied vol down ahead of the weekend, pre-collecting the two dead days, then mark it back up Monday morning. **The weekend's decay was sold to you in advance** - your entry price already reflects it. Realized variance happens on trading days, and the market prices variance, not calendar time.
cards.depth: The transferable rule: a decay everyone can see on a calendar is a decay already in the price. Same reason the ex-div drop hands put holders nothing - a scheduled, universally visible move gets built into the quote before you arrive. Weekend theta is real only in the model.

cards.hook: Daily bars can't tell you if your stop fired first.
cards.body: A daily bar records open, high, low, and close - not the order prices happened in. If your backtest holds a position with a stop below and a target above, and one bar's range touches both, the code must guess which was hit first. Most frameworks quietly assume the favorable order, **crediting wins that were actually stops**. Over hundreds of trades that one assumption compounds into a strategy that never existed. Two fixes: rerun the logic on intraday data, or force the pessimistic order - stop always fires first - and see whether the edge survives.
cards.depth: The same path-blindness poisons anything intrabar: trailing stops, limit entries with same-day exits, short-option strategies with defensive triggers. Rule of thumb: if two of your order levels can sit inside a single bar's range, your bar interval is too coarse for the logic you're testing.

cards.hook: The strongest voice-clone precedent is a 1988 car commercial.
cards.body: When Bette Midler refused Ford's ad campaign, the agency hired her former backup singer and told her to sound exactly like Midler. The Ninth Circuit held that deliberately imitating a distinctive, widely known voice for commercial gain violates California's right of publicity. The doctrinal key still doing the work in AI disputes: **a voice is not copyrightable**, so copyright preemption never blocks the claim - vocal identity is not copyright subject matter. Tom Waits won on the same theory against Frito-Lay in 1992. Today's voice-clone demand letters stand on those two sound-alike cases.
cards.depth: The practitioner error is drafting around the recording. A license to the master covers the copyrighted fixation; it says nothing about synthesizing the performer's vocal identity into new speech. Paper the identity grant separately - which is exactly what the recent digital-replica statutes now force onto the page.

cards.hook: Pre-task motivation is broken. In-task motivation mostly works.
cards.body: Imaging studies of ADHD repeatedly report blunted anticipatory reward signaling: the dopamine response that fires while looking forward to a task runs weak, while reward on contact with the task is closer to intact. That asymmetry means "I'll start when I feel like it" is a plan that structurally never triggers - **the feeling is scheduled to arrive after initiation, not before**. So engineer the start as a mechanical act: open the file, set a five-minute floor, body-double. Treat pre-start dread as noise from a miscalibrated gauge, not as information about the task.
cards.depth: This is why finished tasks so often feel fine in retrospect - "that took twenty minutes, why did I circle it for three days?" The circling was the anticipatory system underselling the reward; the twenty minutes was the intact in-task system doing its job. That recorded gap is the argument for ignoring the forecast.

cards.hook: Praise seemed to backfire. It was just regression.
cards.body: Kahneman's flight instructors were certain: praise a cadet's excellent landing and the next one is worse; scream after a terrible one and the next improves. They concluded criticism works and praise harms. The real driver was arithmetic. An extreme performance is partly luck, so the next attempt drifts back toward the pilot's average **regardless of anything the instructor said**. Because we intervene precisely at the extremes, regression to the mean systematically manufactures evidence that punishment works and reward fails - in coaching, in doubling down after a losing streak, in judging a new associate off one bad memo.
cards.depth: The screen: before crediting any intervention applied after an outlier, ask what the next observation would have looked like with no intervention at all. If selection into treatment was triggered by the extreme itself, regression guarantees improvement-shaped noise either way.

cards.hook: A calendar spread bets on the vol curve, not the stock.
cards.body: Sell the near-dated option, buy the far-dated one at the same strike, and your P&L barely cares where the underlying lands near expiration. What you actually own is a position in the **term structure of implied volatility**. The near leg decays faster and carries lower vega than the far leg. So you profit when the front rolls down and the curve stays upward-sloping, and you bleed when a vol spike lifts the front more than the back, flattening or inverting the curve. Direction is the noise; the shape of the curve is the trade.
cards.depth: The tell is earnings. A calendar placed across an earnings date looks cheap because front-month IV is inflated, but that elevated front vega is exactly what collapses at the print. You end up short the event you appear to be waiting for.

cards.hook: SAG-AFTRA splits your digital double into two legal animals.
cards.body: The 2023 SAG-AFTRA contract does not treat 'AI replica' as one thing. It separates an **Employment-Based Digital Replica**, built from what a performer shoots on the job, from an Independently Created Digital Replica, a synthetic performer assembled from other material. Each carries its own consent rules, and the throughline is that a vague grant fails. Consent must be clear, conspicuous, and tied to a reasonably specific description of how the replica gets used. A studio cannot bury 'we may create and exploit your digital replica' in boilerplate and call it settled.
cards.depth: Practitioners keep drafting one broad replica clause for every situation. That is the error. The consent clearing an on-set body scan does not automatically cover a fully synthetic version used in a project the performer never worked on. Match the clause to the animal.

cards.hook: A good decision can still hand you a bad outcome.
cards.body: Judging a choice by how it turned out is called **resulting**, and it quietly wrecks how you learn. A sound bet with positive expected value can lose; a reckless one can win. Grade the decision by the result and you will punish good process after unlucky losses and reward bad process after lucky wins. Over enough repetitions the luck averages out, but your conclusions do not, because each time you updated on the wrong signal. The fix is to score the decision against what you knew when you made it, not against the card that flipped.
cards.depth: This is why a single blown trade or lost motion tells you almost nothing. To separate skill from variance you need the reasoning written down before the outcome, so you cannot quietly rewrite it to fit the result. Memory is a resulting machine.

cards.hook: Your backtest knows earnings the company hadn't reported yet.
cards.body: Fundamental data gets restated. The revenue or earnings figure you pull for 2015 today is often not the number the market actually saw in 2015, because companies revise and databases overwrite the original with the corrected value. Backtest a signal on those current figures and you are trading on **information that did not exist at the time**. This is look-ahead bias wearing a respectable suit, and it flatters value and quality signals especially, since restatements tend to move in predictable directions. The defense is a point-in-time database that stores what was known on each date, not just the latest truth.
cards.depth: The same trap hits index membership, credit ratings, and analyst estimates. Anything that can be revised after the fact will be, and most vendors keep only the final version. If you cannot get point-in-time data, lag your fundamentals by a quarter or two as a crude guard.

cards.hook: One 1944 lawsuit capped every studio contract at seven years.
cards.body: Studios used to own actors. A standard contract ran seven years, but every time a star refused a role the studio suspended her and tacked the suspension onto the end, so seven years could stretch toward indefinite servitude. Olivia de Havilland sued Warner Bros. and won: a California court ruled that the seven-year limit in Labor Code section 2855 means **seven calendar years, not seven years of actual work**. Suspensions could no longer extend the term. Overnight the studios' most powerful leash on talent went slack, and the star system began shifting toward the people on screen.
cards.depth: The rule still bites. Section 2855 is why recording artists and other personal-service talent can walk after seven years, and why long-term deals get restructured to survive it. A 1944 fight over film roles quietly governs contract length across California entertainment today.

cards.hook: Exercising a call early burns money, except the night before ex-div.
cards.body: An American call is almost always worth more alive than dead: selling it captures extrinsic value that exercising burns. The one exception comes the night before an ex-dividend date. Exercise then and you own the stock for the dividend; hold, and the shares open lower by roughly the dividend while your call just eats the drop. The test is mechanical: **exercise only when the dividend exceeds the call's remaining extrinsic value**. Deep in-the-money calls on big-dividend names get swept this way every quarter, so if you are short them, expect assignment the night before ex-div, not at expiration.
cards.depth: The mirror trade exists on the put side: with no dividend to chase, early put exercise is about collecting interest on the strike, which is why deep puts started disappearing early again once rates left zero. Either way the driver is carry, never sentiment.

cards.hook: The WGA never banned AI. It made AI output creditless.
cards.body: The 2023 WGA agreement's core move was definitional. AI-generated material is neither 'literary material' nor 'source material' under the contract. That sounds technical until you remember the credit system runs on those two terms: a writer rewriting AI text is not adapting source material, so they keep full writing credit and full compensation, with no 'based on' discount. **AI output cannot be used to erode credit or pay.** Studios must also disclose when material they hand a writer is AI-generated, and cannot require a writer to use AI. No ban, just a contract that strips AI text of its leverage.
cards.depth: Compare SAG-AFTRA's 2023 deal, which took the opposite architecture: consent plus compensation for digital replicas rather than definitional exclusion. Two guilds, two templates, and private AI riders now borrow from both, exclusion language for authorship questions, consent-and-pay language for likeness.

cards.hook: A gram of vitamin C can shorten your medication's day.
cards.body: Once lisdexamfetamine converts, getting rid of d-amphetamine is your kidneys' job, and amphetamine is a weak base. In acidic urine it ionizes, cannot be reabsorbed, and washes out quickly; in alkaline urine the kidney keeps reclaiming it into the blood. Reported elimination half-lives swing several-fold across that pH range. **The same dose can run short or long depending on urine chemistry.** The prescribing labels warn in both directions: urinary acidifiers, including gram-dose vitamin C, cut drug levels, while alkalinizers like sodium bicarbonate raise them. If afternoon coverage reliably dies early, raise the pH question with your prescriber before concluding the dose failed.
