cards.depth: This is excretion, not absorption. The rate-limited enzymatic conversion still caps the peak, so pH mostly stretches or trims the tail of the day. And never self-alkalinize to extend duration: bicarbonate loading spikes amphetamine levels unpredictably, which is exactly why the interaction sits on the label.

cards.hook: The trades were right. Everyone knowing them was fatal.
cards.body: LTCM's trades were mostly sound convergence bets, off-the-run versus on-the-run Treasuries, merger spreads, short long-dated equity vol, levered roughly 25-to-1. When Russia defaulted in August 1998 the spreads blew out, but what killed the fund was that its book was an open secret. Counterparties could infer the positions, mark them down, and trade ahead of the forced unwind, so every attempt to cut risk moved prices further away. About $4.6 billion evaporated in under four months before the Fed corralled fourteen banks into a $3.6 billion takeover. **A position everyone can see becomes its own risk factor.** Most of the spreads later converged, profitably, for the banks.
cards.depth: The structural lesson beats the math lesson: the models priced the trades, never the holders. Crowding and financing terms set your survival horizon, and convergence that arrives after the margin call belongs to someone else. Niederhoffer, Amaranth, and the 2018 short-vol funds all rhyme: plausible thesis, wrong balance sheet.

cards.hook: Recall it: why did 200,000 birds cost the same as 2,000?
cards.body: Before scrolling: what is the mind actually pricing when it answers a save-the-birds question? Hold your answer for a beat. The study found people paid roughly the same to save 2,000, 20,000, or 200,000 birds, because the mind never multiplies. It answers a **prototype question instead of a quantity one**: it summons one oil-soaked bird, prices the feeling, and returns that figure whatever the count. Scope insensitivity.
cards.depth: The reuse test: any time a valuation should scale with magnitude, damages, charitable impact, the size of a tail you can vividly picture, check whether you priced the image or the quantity. If your number would survive a tenfold change in scope, you priced the image. Multiply on paper, deliberately.

cards.hook: Delta is not your probability of finishing in the money.
cards.body: The retail shorthand treats a 16-delta short put as an 84% winner. But delta is N(d1); the probability of expiring in the money is N(d2), and d2 is always lower. For puts that cuts against you: the chance of finishing ITM is N(-d2), which is **higher than the delta you sold**. The gap between the two is vol times root-time - negligible on a weekly at 15% vol, real on 45-90 day options in elevated vol, large on LEAPS. Delta is a hedge ratio, not a forecast; it overweights the states where the option pays more.
cards.depth: Mechanically, delta is the ITM probability under a different measure - one that uses the stock itself as the unit of account, which tilts weight toward high-price paths. N(d2) is the risk-neutral probability. And both differ from the real-world probability, which nobody quotes you.

cards.hook: Don't trade the best parameter. Trade its neighborhood.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="40" y1="210" x2="370" y2="210" stroke="#35302a" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="40" y1="30" x2="40" y2="210" stroke="#35302a" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M50 200 C110 195 130 110 200 105 C270 110 300 195 360 200" fill="none" stroke="#7fb4a2" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M50 205 L130 200 L148 55 L166 200 L360 205" fill="none" stroke="#d9a441" stroke-width="3"/><text x="160" y="52" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14">one lucky spike</text><text x="210" y="92" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14">plateau = robust edge</text><text x="150" y="232" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13">parameter value</text><text x="46" y="24" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13">backtest P&L</text></svg>
cards.body: If a 21-day lookback makes money while 18 and 25 lose, you have not found a signal; you have found the one setting that fit the noise. A real effect is rarely precise about its own parameters - momentum that works at 21 days should still work, degraded, at 15 and at 30. So plot P&L across the whole parameter range and **buy the plateau, not the peak**. Some quants go further and deliberately trade a slightly off-peak setting, accepting a worse backtest for a number the optimizer didn't hand-pick.
cards.depth: This is a cheap visual defense that complements walk-forward testing: walk-forward asks whether the edge survives time, the plateau asks whether it survives specification. A strategy that fails the plateau test usually fails out of sample for the same reason - the peak was sampling error.

cards.hook: One repealed FCC rule explains why backend died.
cards.body: From 1970 to the mid-90s, the fin-syn rules barred ABC, CBS and NBC from taking a financial interest in the prime-time shows they aired, or from syndicating them. Networks were forced to be renters, so studios and independent producers kept ownership - and syndication backend built the Cosby and Seinfeld fortunes. The FCC phased the rules out by 1995. Within months Disney bought ABC, and within a decade every network sat inside a studio. **Self-dealing replaced the arm's-length license fee**, and the streamer cost-plus buyout is that logic completed: the buyer owns the show, so there is nothing left to syndicate.
cards.depth: The rhyme runs backward too. Fin-syn answered an earlier consolidation - three networks squeezing producers much as the pre-1948 studios had squeezed exhibitors before the Paramount decrees. Regulation forced fragmentation, deregulation restored integration, and the profit-participation definitions tracked the structure each time.

cards.hook: Hitchcock: surprise buys fifteen seconds, suspense buys fifteen minutes.
cards.body: Hitchcock's bomb theory: two people chat, a bomb under the table explodes - the audience gets fifteen seconds of surprise. Let them see the bomb and the timer first, and the same banal conversation becomes unbearable for fifteen minutes. Suspense is not withheld information; it is **information the characters don't have**. The working move: when a scene feels flat, stop hiding things from the audience and start hiding them from the characters. Withholding builds a puzzle; disclosure builds dread. Most drafts default to the puzzle because it is easier to write.
cards.depth: Hitchcock's corollary: the bomb must almost never go off. The audience carried the knowledge, so they must be relieved, not punished for participating. He broke the rule once, in Sabotage (1936), letting the bomb kill a boy - and told Truffaut it was a mistake.

cards.hook: Every system you build will stop working. Budget for that.
cards.body: The planner that worked in March and the app that worked in June did not fail because you got lazy. Novelty itself was doing load-bearing work: a new tool has salience, and salience recruits attention when top-down effort is unreliable. As novelty habituates, the tool goes invisible - same object, less signal. So stop searching for the permanent system and **rotate on purpose**: keep the data portable (plain text, one folder), treat any capture tool as a roughly 90-day appliance, and swap the container before it dies instead of after. The system is the rotation, not the app.
cards.depth: This reframes the graveyard of abandoned tools: decay is the expected trajectory, so a dead tool is a completed tour of duty, not evidence you cannot maintain things. What must persist is the externalized data; what can churn is the interface pointing at it.

cards.hook: Recall it: what does rolling a loser for a credit really do?
cards.body: Before the answer: that credit came from somewhere. The market does not pay you to fix mistakes, so what did you sell to get it? Here it is: you closed the losing trade at a loss and opened a new, larger one, and the credit exists only because you added duration, size, or a closer strike. **A roll is re-entry at worse odds, not repair.** The test survives a second telling: if you would not open the new position fresh today, with no loss attached to it, you have no business rolling into it.
cards.depth: Why this one recurs: your broker displays the roll as one continuing position, which quietly converts a realized loss into an unrealized one. That accounting illusion is the whole seduction. Book the loss mentally at the moment you roll, and the decision gets honest again.

cards.hook: Backtest today's index members and you've excluded the corpses.
cards.body: Build your universe from current S&P 500 membership and you are testing on companies certified, in hindsight, as survivors. The index swaps out roughly 20 to 25 constituents a year, so over a 20-year backtest hundreds of delisted, acquired, and bankrupt names simply vanish from your sample. Any strategy that buys weakness looks brilliant, because the stocks that fell and never got up are not there to hurt it. **The dead are missing from your data.** The fix is point-in-time constituent lists: test each date against the membership that existed on that date, corpses included.
cards.depth: Survivorship bias flatters mean-reversion and value strategies most, since those deliberately hold losers. The mutual-fund literature found the same thing one level up: databases that quietly dropped dead funds overstated average returns by enough to change conclusions. If your data vendor cannot answer 'as of when,' assume the bias is in.

cards.hook: The studios finally sued an AI company, and skipped training entirely.
cards.body: In June 2025 Disney and Universal filed the first major-studio copyright suit against a generative AI company, targeting Midjourney. Notice what the complaint does not lead with: training data. The theory is output-side - the tool serves up recognizable Darth Vader, Minions, and Shrek on demand, a 'virtual vending machine' of infringing copies, in the complaint's phrase. That routes around the ingestion fair-use fight, where AI defendants had been landing wins, and into **character infringement, doctrine studios have been winning on for decades.** An output claim does not care how the model learned, only what it emits.
cards.depth: The complaint also alleges Midjourney kept generating the characters after the studios requested filters other AI firms had implemented - a willfulness record built before filing. Drafting note: AI reps and indemnities keyed only to training-data provenance miss this entire vector. Output is its own exposure and needs its own language.

cards.hook: Two underwriters, same file. Their quotes differed by half.
cards.body: Bias is the average error; noise is the scatter. In a noise audit Kahneman and colleagues reported from a large insurer, executives guessed that two underwriters quoting the identical case would differ by about 10%. The reported median difference was roughly 55%. Nobody had noticed, because judgment noise is invisible in the wild: each case gets one judge, so the disagreement never surfaces. **You cannot see noise in a single verdict.** Settlement valuations, damages estimates, price targets - anywhere professionals produce a number from a file, assume the scatter is several times what the institution believes.
cards.depth: The cheap fixes are mechanical: collect independent estimates before anyone speaks, average them, and score the components of the judgment separately before the overall call. Averaging independent judgments cancels noise directly. It does nothing for shared bias, which is exactly why the two errors need different medicine.

cards.hook: Your last task follows you into this one.
cards.body: Sophie Leroy's research on attention residue: when you switch tasks, part of your attention stays behind with the one you left, degrading performance on the task in front of you - and the residue is worst when the prior task was unfinished. That is a working-memory tax an ADHD brain can least afford, stacked on an already expensive switch. The move is a ready-to-resume note: before switching, spend 30 seconds writing exactly where you stopped and the literal next action. **Park the open loop in writing, not in your head.** Leroy's follow-up work found this brief ritual reduces residue and speeds re-engagement.
cards.depth: Mechanism, not vibes: unfinished goals stay active and keep intruding (the old Zeigarnik findings point the same direction). The written note externalizes the open loop - the same principle as keeping the to-do list outside your head. Working memory is for processing, not for holding state across an interruption.

cards.hook: Friday's option prices have already spent the weekend.
cards.body: Option models spread theta smoothly across calendar days, but market makers do not wait around for days with no trading. Into Friday's close they mark implied vol down, pre-collecting the two dead days, then mark it back up Monday morning. So a Friday short sale that looks like it harvests three days of decay is mostly buying a vol level that already reflects them. **The weekend's decay is sold in advance.** The clean way to see it: realized variance happens on trading days, and the market prices variance, not calendar time. Weekend theta is real only in the model.
cards.depth: The same markdown appears around holidays, and in reverse around scheduled events: earnings and CPI days carry extra implied variance while dead days carry almost none. Desks that quote in business time rather than calendar time avoid the illusion entirely. If your backtest credits full calendar theta over weekends, it is overstating short-premium returns.

cards.hook: Run a hundred backtests, and the best one lies.
cards.body: Suppose every strategy you test is pure noise. Test one hundred, and the best in-sample Sharpe will still look excellent, because you selected it for exactly that. The maximum of many noisy estimates is biased upward, and the bias grows with the number of trials. The reported number is not the strategy's Sharpe; it is **the winner of a tournament you ran against randomness**. Honest practice: count every variant you tried, including the ones you abandoned, discount the winner for the size of the field, or validate it on data the selection never touched.
cards.depth: Bailey and Lopez de Prado formalized the discount as the deflated Sharpe ratio, which asks whether your best result clears the bar you would expect from N tries on noise alone. Most published backtests fail that bar, which is one reason live performance so reliably disappoints.

cards.hook: The record AI copyright settlement wasn't about training at all.
cards.body: In September 2025 Anthropic agreed to pay roughly 1.5 billion dollars, reported as the largest copyright settlement ever, to authors whose books sat in its training data. The part practitioners keep missing: the court had already ruled that training on lawfully purchased books was fair use. What survived was the claim over books downloaded from pirate libraries. Liability turned on **how the copies were acquired, not what the model learned**. The drafting lesson for anyone papering AI deals: point the warranties and diligence at data provenance, the acquisition chain, because that is where the money actually moved.
cards.depth: Reported terms ran near 3,000 dollars per work across roughly half a million titles, with the pirated copies destroyed. Compare Thomson Reuters v. Ross, where training use lost outright: the fair-use question is still unsettled circuit by circuit, but the piracy question is not, and it prices at scale.

cards.hook: Recall it: why must your to-do list live outside your head?
cards.body: Two weeks ago this feed made a claim about which cognitive function ADHD taxes hardest, and what it costs to keep a plan in your head. Name the function and the move before reading on. The function is working memory. Holding your next three steps active burns the same buffer that executing the current step requires, so the held items crowd out the doing. The move: **offload every open loop to one external surface** the instant it appears. One surface, not five apps. Capture is not tidiness; it frees the scarce resource to run the task actually in front of you.
cards.depth: Retrieval strengthens memory more than rereading does, which is why this card asks before it tells. The live test two weeks on is behavioral, not conceptual: does capture happen at the moment the thought arrives? A system consulted later but not fed in the moment protects nothing.

cards.hook: Negotiate every issue at once, never one at a time.
cards.body: Issue-by-issue bargaining quietly converts a deal into a series of zero-sum fights: each point gets contested on its own, and you spend goodwill winning things you barely value. Package bargaining changes the math. Put every open issue on the table together and you can **trade across differences in priorities**: concede what is cheap to you and expensive to them, and take the reverse. Negotiation researchers push it further with multiple equivalent simultaneous offers, presenting two or three packages you value identically. Which package the counterparty pulls toward reveals their priorities without them saying a word.
cards.depth: The equal-value part is the discipline. If the packages differ in value to you, you have just made three offers and invited cherry-picking. Built honestly, simultaneous packages also read as flexible, which the research links to better counterpart satisfaction at no cost to your own outcome.

cards.hook: In contango, time alone rolls your VIX short into profit.
cards.body: VIX futures usually sit above spot, a shape called contango. If nothing else changes, each future must still fall toward the lower cash VIX as expiry approaches. Short the future and that convergence pays you even when volatility is flat. **The roll yield, not a vol forecast, is most of the return** in a short-vol carry trade. The exposure is dangerously one-sided: the same position that quietly harvests calm-day carry takes the full blow the moment the curve flips into backwardation and spot spikes above the futures you are short.
cards.depth: This is why short-vol carry looks like free money for years and then isn't. You are paid a small, steady premium for absorbing a rare, violent tail. Any strategy whose P&L is dominated by roll yield is selling insurance, and the payout you dread is precisely the event the premium was supposedly compensating you for.

cards.hook: Copyright protects only the parts of AI art you authored.
cards.body: The US Copyright Office's 2025 guidance holds that purely AI-generated output has no human author, so it gets no protection at all. What survives is your **selectable, arrangeable human contribution**: text you wrote, the sequence you chose, edits you made by hand. In the Zarya of the Dawn comic, the Office kept the writer's story and page layout but stripped protection from the Midjourney images themselves. Prompting, however elaborate, was treated as requesting a result rather than authoring one. The generated image, on its own, belongs to no one.
cards.depth: The commercial fallout is real: an AI-heavy ad or piece of key art can be freely copied, because the machine-made pixels sit in the public domain the instant they exist. Protect the deal by contracting over the human-authored elements and by building in genuine editing passes that leave a documentable authorship trail.

cards.hook: You'd pay about the same to save 2,000 birds or 200,000.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><line x1="40" y1="200" x2="370" y2="200" stroke="#35302a"/><rect x="70" y="90" width="50" height="110" fill="#d9a441"/><rect x="180" y="92" width="50" height="108" fill="#d9a441"/><rect x="290" y="84" width="50" height="116" fill="#d9a441"/><text x="95" y="218" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">2,000</text><text x="205" y="218" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">20,000</text><text x="315" y="218" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">200,000 birds</text><text x="200" y="38" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle">100x the birds, same willingness to pay</text></svg>
cards.body: In a classic study, people asked what they'd pay to save migrating birds from oil ponds gave roughly the same figure whether the toll was 2,000, 20,000, or 200,000. The mind does not multiply. It answers a **prototype question instead of a quantity one**: it pictures one oil-soaked bird, prices that feeling, and ignores the count entirely. This is scope insensitivity, and it quietly wrecks any valuation driven by magnitude, from charitable giving to jury damages to how you size a vivid, low-probability tail you can easily imagine.
cards.depth: The trading version: a story about one catastrophic scenario feels equally frightening at 2% or 0.2%, so you overpay for hedges priced off vividness rather than frequency. The correction is mechanical. Force the number back in, because expected value is count times consequence, and your gut handed you only the consequence.

cards.hook: Make time take up space you can physically see.
cards.body: ADHD blunts the internal sense of time passing, so a deadline three hours out feels the same as three days out, right up until it is suddenly now. The move is to **externalize duration into something visual**: a countdown that shows remaining time as a shrinking colored wedge, not digits. Digits still make you compute how much is left, a working-memory step you keep skipping. A shrinking area is perceived directly, no computation required, so the passage of time registers as a physical event happening in front of you instead of an abstract fact you forget to check.
cards.depth: The principle scales. A wall calendar you can't avoid seeing beats a phone calendar you must decide to open. Any executive function you are weak at should be moved out of your head and into the environment, where raw perception does the monitoring your internal clock refuses to do.

cards.hook: A precise first offer anchors harder than a round one.
cards.body: Round numbers read as placeholders. Open at $10,000 and the other side hears "around ten, negotiable." Open at $9,850 and they infer you did actual math, that the figure rests on something, and they **adjust in smaller increments away from your anchor**. Research on anchor precision reports that counteroffers land closer to a precise opening and the final split tilts toward whoever set it. The precision itself signals information you may not even possess, which is why a lazy round counter so often concedes ground before a single term has actually been argued.
cards.depth: Use it on purpose. When you open, pick a defensible non-round number and be ready to explain it, because a precise anchor you can't justify invites the "where did that come from" challenge that resets the frame back to round. Precision is a claim of knowledge. Make sure the claim is real.

cards.hook: Short-dated options are gamma bets; long-dated ones are vega bets.
cards.body: Gamma and vega both scale with time to expiry, but in opposite directions. Gamma runs with the inverse square root of time, so a near-dated option whips around with spot. Vega runs with the square root of time, so a far-dated option reprices hard when implied vol shifts. **A weekly short strangle and a two-year one are different animals with the same name.** The weekly's real risk is a gap in the underlying. The LEAP's real risk is a repricing of volatility you may hold for months.
cards.depth: This is why front-month sellers obsess over pin risk and gaps, while long-dated sellers obsess over the vol surface. Same trade name, different greek doing the damage. Size and hedge to the greek that actually dominates your expiry, not the one the strategy label implies.

cards.hook: Tennessee made your voice a property right against AI.
cards.body: Tennessee's old publicity law, written in the Elvis era, protected name, photograph, and likeness. The 2024 ELVIS Act adds voice explicitly, and goes further: it targets the tools. **Liability reaches anyone who distributes software whose primary purpose is cloning a person's voice or likeness without consent.** Most publicity statutes only reach the party who commercially exploits the fake. This one reaches the maker of the generator itself. It took effect July 1, 2024, the first US law aimed squarely at generative voice cloning.
cards.depth: The practitioner miss is treating it like ordinary right-of-publicity. The toolmaker exposure is new, and it does not require the cloned person to be a celebrity or the use to be commercial in the traditional sense. Watch for other states copying the structure.

cards.hook: Your ADHD med is inert until your blood cuts it apart.
cards.body: Lisdexamfetamine is d-amphetamine chemically bonded to the amino acid lysine. Swallowed, it is pharmacologically inert. Enzymes in your red blood cells slowly cleave off the lysine, releasing active drug at a pace the enzyme controls, not your gut. **The conversion is rate-limited, so the peak stays capped and the curve stays smooth.** Practical reads: the route cannot cheat it, crushing or snorting does nothing; food barely shifts timing; and raising the dose mostly stretches the area under the curve rather than sharpening the spike.
cards.depth: This is why titration feels gradual instead of a switch flipping, and why a too-low dose reads as 'barely noticeable' rather than wrong. The design trades a fast, abusable peak for a steady one. Judge a dose over weeks at steady state, not on day three.

cards.hook: Perfect calibration can still make you a useless forecaster.
cards.body: Predict the base rate every time. Say 30 percent for every applicant when 30 percent succeed, and over enough trials you are perfectly calibrated: your 30 percent calls come true 30 percent of the time. But you have said nothing useful, because you cannot separate winners from losers. The missing quality is **resolution**, the willingness to move off the base rate when you actually know something. The Brier score splits into exactly these two parts. Superforecasters win on resolution, pushing to 5 and 95 and being right, not on calibration alone.
cards.depth: Calibration is table stakes and easy to fake by hugging the base rate. Resolution is the hard, valuable part, and it is where information actually lives. When you score your own trading or legal calls, track both, or you will reward timid forecasts that never risk being wrong.

cards.hook: Where in a long prompt does a model quietly lose your instruction?
cards.body: Think back to the U-shaped attention card. Models attend most to the very start and the very end of a context, and sag in the middle. Take a beat before the answer: the danger zone is **the middle**. Bury a load-bearing constraint halfway through a long context and it gets underweighted, even though it is technically present and retrievable. The researchers called it 'lost in the middle.' So put the task and the constraints that must hold at the top or the bottom, never in the soft center.
cards.depth: It matters again every time you paste a long document and tack 'and remember to do X' at the end. That lands in a strong position by luck; move it there on purpose. As contexts grow longer, the middle sag deepens, so the habit pays more the bigger your prompts get.

cards.hook: Short volatility pays you monthly, then bills you all at once.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="10" y1="140" x2="390" y2="140" stroke="#35302a"/><rect x="20" y="120" width="16" height="20" fill="#7fb4a2"/><rect x="44" y="122" width="16" height="18" fill="#7fb4a2"/><rect x="68" y="119" width="16" height="21" fill="#7fb4a2"/><rect x="92" y="123" width="16" height="17" fill="#7fb4a2"/><rect x="116" y="120" width="16" height="20" fill="#7fb4a2"/><rect x="140" y="121" width="16" height="19" fill="#7fb4a2"/><rect x="164" y="119" width="16" height="21" fill="#7fb4a2"/><rect x="188" y="122" width="16" height="18" fill="#7fb4a2"/><rect x="212" y="120" width="16" height="20" fill="#7fb4a2"/><rect x="236" y="121" width="16" height="19" fill="#7fb4a2"/><rect x="260" y="120" width="16" height="20" fill="#7fb4a2"/><rect x="302" y="140" width="34" height="78" fill="#d9a441"/><text x="20" y="110" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13">small wins, most months</text><text x="282" y="232" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13">one month gives it back</text></svg>
cards.body: The variance risk premium is real, but its payoff is **negatively skewed**: a long run of small wins punctuated by rare, violent losses. Most months implied exceeds realized and you collect. Then one regime break hands back a year of premium in a week. This shape is why the Sharpe ratio flatters short-vol books. It rewards smooth upside and barely penalizes the fat left tail until the tail actually arrives. Sizing has to assume the loss month, not the median month.
cards.depth: The same skew defends the premium. If short vol paid smoothly, capital would flood in and compete it away. The pain of the tail is the barrier to entry, so the wage exists precisely because the ride is not smooth.

cards.hook: The first AI fair-use ruling went against the machine.
cards.body: In February 2025, Judge Bibas granted summary judgment to **Thomson Reuters** against Ross Intelligence, holding that copying Westlaw headnotes to train a legal-research tool was not fair use. Two things made it bite. The AI was non-generative, so it competed directly with the source instead of transforming it. And factor four, market harm, cut hard: Ross built a market substitute for Westlaw. Practitioners over-read it as a template for the generative cases. Bibas expressly noted his reasoning may not carry to systems that output new expression.
cards.depth: The same judge had denied summary judgment in 2023 and set the case for trial, then reversed himself on reconsideration. That reversal is the tell. Courts are still finding their footing, and an early ruling is a data point, not settled doctrine.

cards.hook: Your 90% confidence ranges are right about half the time.
cards.body: Ask people for a range they are 90% sure contains the answer, and the true value falls inside only **roughly 40 to 60%** of the time. The interval comes out too narrow because its width itself signals ignorance, and admitting ignorance feels like weakness. The fix is mechanical, not motivational: widen every interval until it feels slightly embarrassing, then widen once more. Calibration is a trainable skill, and the cheapest edge in any forecast is refusing to be as sure as you feel.
cards.depth: This is why point estimates lie. "It'll cost 40k" hides the range. Forcing an explicit low and high, then stretching both, surfaces the tail you were pretending away, and the tail is usually where the decision actually lives.

cards.hook: Pre-decide the trigger, not just the task.
cards.body: A to-do names what to do but leaves the hardest part, when and where, to a moment when your executive function is already taxed. **Implementation intentions** close that gap: you write "if situation X, then I do Y." When the trigger arrives, the action fires with far less deliberation, because you offloaded the decision to a rule instead of your working memory. Reported effect sizes across dozens of studies run medium to large. It works best for exactly the tasks you keep meaning to start and never do.
cards.depth: "When I sit down with coffee, I open the deal doc first" beats "review the deal doc." The cue does the initiating your brain won't. Attach the new action to something you already do reliably, and the existing habit becomes the trigger.

cards.hook: A week back, how many items does working memory really hold?
cards.body: The famous number is seven, from Miller's 1956 paper. The **better answer is about four**, per Cowan's later work, and often fewer once the items are unfamiliar or you are tired. This is not trivia for you. It is the whole case for externalizing: a checklist, a scratchpad, one visible next step. If the plan lives only in your head, you are asking a four-slot buffer to hold six things, and it will silently drop two. Put it on paper and the buffer is free to actually think.
cards.depth: Chunking is the loophole. Four chunks of familiar material can each carry a lot, which is why expertise feels like extra memory. It isn't more slots, it's richer contents in each one.

cards.hook: Rolling a loser for a credit is a new, bigger bet.
cards.body: When your short option goes against you, the popular move is to roll it out in time for a net credit, and it feels like you fixed the trade. You did not. You closed one position at a loss and opened a larger, longer-dated one, and the credit only exists because you added duration, size, or moved the strike closer to the money. The market did not hand you money; you sold more risk. **A roll is not repair, it is re-entry at worse odds.** If you would not open that new position fresh today, do not roll into it.
cards.depth: The credit is an accounting artifact: extrinsic value from the added time, minus the intrinsic you just absorbed. Traders anchor on 'never realize a loss,' so they chain rolls until one gap move on an oversized position ends the sequence. The discipline is to price the roll as a standalone trade, blind to the entry you are anchored to.

cards.hook: Using a dead actor's digital replica now needs estate consent.
cards.body: For years California's postmortem right of publicity (Civil Code 3344.1) covered a deceased personality's name, image, and likeness for 70 years, but it predated convincing synthetic performances. AB 1836, operative January 1, 2025, closes that gap: producing an audiovisual work with a digital replica of a deceased performer now requires consent from the estate. **The statute targets the replica specifically, not just the underlying likeness.** So a studio that licensed old footage does not automatically hold the right to generate new AI performances from it. Old grants may not reach synthetic resurrection.
cards.depth: The practitioner trap is treating a footage license or an old NIL grant as blanket authority. AB 1836 wants consent that references the digital replica's use with specificity, and it carves exceptions for news, satire, and documentary. For estates it is a new revenue line; for producers, a new clearance step before any generative resurrection.

cards.hook: Time-based reminders fail you. Event-based ones fire on their own.
cards.body: Prospective memory, remembering to do a thing later, comes in two flavors. Time-based ('call the pharmacy at 3') makes you monitor the clock yourself, which is exactly the self-cueing an ADHD brain does poorly. Event-based ('call the pharmacy when I get in the car') rides a cue the environment delivers for free. The fix is not a better alarm; it is to **anchor the new action to an event that already reliably happens.** After I pour coffee, I take the meds. The trigger stops depending on you noticing time, and starts depending on a thing the world does anyway.
cards.depth: This is Gollwitzer's implementation-intentions research, the 'when-then' plan. It helps everyone but disproportionately those with weak self-directed cueing. Stack the new behavior onto an existing anchor tied to a fixed action or place, never a time. The anchor carries the memory load your prefrontal cortex keeps dropping.

cards.hook: Your signal uses today's close. So does your fill. Impossible.
cards.body: A classic silent look-ahead: your rule says 'buy when today's close is above the 50-day average,' and your backtest fills the buy at today's close. But you cannot know the close until the session ends, and by then you can no longer trade at it. The signal and the execution share a price that exists only after trading stops. **The fix is a one-bar lag: signal on today's close, fill at tomorrow's open.** That single shift often erases most of a strategy's apparent edge, because the edge was living in a fill nobody could actually get.
cards.depth: This is distinct from slippage; the price is not merely optimistic, it is unobtainable in principle. The tell is a strategy whose returns collapse the moment you lag execution by one bar. Any signal built from a bar's own close, high, or low must execute on a later bar, or the backtest is quietly trading with tomorrow's newspaper.

cards.hook: Which is likelier: a bank teller, or a feminist bank teller?
cards.body: Take a beat before you answer. The vivid version, the feminist bank teller, feels more likely because it fits the story you were told about her. But every feminist bank teller is already a bank teller, so that group can only be smaller. **Adding a specific detail can never raise a probability, only lower it.** This is the conjunction fallacy: representativeness, how well a scenario matches a stereotype, hijacks your sense of likelihood. The richer and more convincing the picture, the fewer people it actually describes.
cards.depth: Why it bites you again: every detailed forecast, deal scenario, or risk narrative you find persuasive is paying a probability tax for its specificity. 'The market falls because of X, then Y, then Z' feels rigorous and is strictly less likely than 'the market falls.' Strip the conjunctions before you bet on the story.
